name: Dublin
tagline: Ireland's compact, literary capital, where medieval history, world-class museums and a legendary pub culture sit within an easy walk of each other.
highlight: Standing in the Long Room of Trinity College's Old Library, beneath its barrel-vaulted ceiling and thousands of ancient volumes, feet from the Book of Kells.
shortDescription: Ireland's capital, a compact, walkable city of medieval castles, world-class museums and a legendary pub and music culture.
metaDescription: A Dublin travel guide: Trinity College and the Book of Kells, the Guinness Storehouse, Kilmainham Gaol, food and how to plan a visit to Ireland's capital.
knownFor: Trinity College, the Guinness Storehouse, literary history
goodFor: City culture, history, nightlife and live music

image.file: File:Dubln - River Liffey with Ha'Penny Bridge in distance.jpg
image.alt: The River Liffey and the Ha'penny Bridge in central Dublin

intro: Dublin is one of Europe's most compact capital cities, small enough to cross on foot in under an hour, yet packed with a literary and musical reputation far larger than its size would suggest.

It's also a city of contrasts — a working medieval castle and a Georgian university sit blocks from buzzing Temple Bar pubs, while the Guinness Storehouse and Kilmainham Gaol tell two very different stories about the same small island.

Most visitors use Dublin as the start or end of a wider Ireland trip, and a couple of days here earns that role, offering real context — historical, literary and culinary — for everywhere else on the itinerary.

whyVisit.intro: Dublin's case rests on world-class museums and history packed into a small, easy-to-navigate city.

points.title: Trinity College holds an extraordinary manuscript
points.text: The 9th-century Book of Kells and the Old Library's Long Room are among Europe's most atmospheric sights.

points.title: The Guinness Storehouse is a full sensory experience
points.text: Seven floors built around a single pint, ending with panoramic city views from the rooftop Gravity Bar.

points.title: Kilmainham Gaol tells essential Irish history
points.text: The site of the 1916 Rising leaders' executions, and one of the country's most moving museum experiences.

points.title: It's compact and walkable
points.text: Most major sights sit within a comfortable walk of the city centre, either side of the River Liffey.

points.title: The pub and music culture is the real thing
points.text: Live traditional sessions happen nightly, not just as a tourist performance.

attractionsIntro: Dublin's essential sights combine genuine medieval and Georgian history with world-class museums.

attractions.name: Trinity College & the Book of Kells

image.file: File:Dublin Trinity College Library Long Room Book of Kells 1.jpg
image.alt: The Long Room of the Old Library at Trinity College Dublin

attractions.text: Ireland's oldest university, home to the illuminated 9th-century Book of Kells and the barrel-vaulted Long Room lined with ancient volumes.
attractions.tip: Book timed tickets online ahead — the Long Room sells out, especially in summer.

attractions.name: Guinness Storehouse

image.alt: The Guinness Storehouse building in Dublin

attractions.text: An immersive seven-floor experience built around Ireland's most famous export, ending with a pint and a view from the rooftop Gravity Bar.
attractions.tip: The rooftop bar offers one of Dublin's best panoramic views, included with entry.

attractions.name: Dublin Castle

image.file: File:Chapel Royal Interior 1, Dublin Castle, Dublin, Ireland - Diliff.jpg
image.alt: The ornate interior of the Chapel Royal at Dublin Castle

attractions.text: A still-functioning seat of Irish state ceremony, its state apartments and Chapel Royal open to visitors between official events.
attractions.tip: Check ahead — the state apartments occasionally close for official functions.

attractions.name: Kilmainham Gaol

image.alt: The vaulted main hall of Kilmainham Gaol in Dublin

attractions.text: A powerful former prison where leaders of the 1916 Easter Rising were executed, now a museum central to modern Irish history.
attractions.tip: Book well ahead — tours are guided-only and regularly sell out days in advance.

attractions.name: St Patrick's Cathedral

image.file: File:St Patrick's Cathedral Exterior, Dublin, Ireland - Diliff.jpg
image.alt: The exterior of St Patrick's Cathedral in Dublin

attractions.text: Ireland's largest church, founded in 1191, with connections to Jonathan Swift, who served as dean here for over 30 years.
attractions.tip: The choral evensong, held most weekdays, is free and atmospheric.

attractions.name: Phoenix Park

image.file: File:Phoenix Park is an urban park in Dublin, Ireland (5489563092).jpg
image.alt: The open parkland of Phoenix Park in Dublin

attractions.text: A vast city park, more than twice the size of New York's Central Park, home to a herd of wild fallow deer and the President's residence.
attractions.tip: Rent a bike to cover the park's full size — it's larger than it first appears.

attractions.name: Temple Bar

image.file: File:Picture of The Temple Bar in Dublin - Photo du bar The Temple Bar à Dublin.jpg
image.alt: The colourful Temple Bar pub in Dublin's Temple Bar district

attractions.text: Dublin's best-known nightlife quarter, cobbled lanes packed with pubs, live music and a lively, touristy energy after dark.
attractions.tip: Prices run higher here than elsewhere — a few streets over often means a quieter, cheaper pint.

thingsToDoIntro: Dublin rewards mixing its major museums with a wander through its riverside and parkland.

thingsToDo.title: Cross the Ha'penny Bridge

image.alt: The Ha'penny Bridge over the River Liffey in Dublin

thingsToDo.text: An essential Dublin moment, crossing the elegant cast-iron footbridge that has linked the city's two halves since 1816.
thingsToDo.tip: The bridge and riverbanks are especially atmospheric lit up after dark.

thingsToDo.title: Shop and stroll Grafton Street

image.alt: Grafton Street, Dublin's pedestrianised shopping street

thingsToDo.text: A lively pedestrianised street of shops, cafés and buskers, running from Trinity College to St Stephen's Green.
thingsToDo.tip: Street performers here are often excellent — worth stopping for a few minutes.

thingsToDo.title: Relax in St Stephen's Green

image.alt: St Stephen's Green, a Victorian park in central Dublin

thingsToDo.text: A peaceful Victorian park right in the city centre, a good spot to pause between museums and shopping streets.
thingsToDo.tip: Free and open year-round, with a bandstand hosting occasional summer concerts.

thingsToDo.title: Day-trip to Howth
thingsToDo.text: An easy DART train ride to a working fishing village with cliff walks, seafood and views back across Dublin Bay.
thingsToDo.tip: The cliff path loop takes about two hours and needs no special gear.

thingsToDo.title: Catch a live trad session
thingsToDo.text: A nightly occurrence in pubs across the city, informal sessions of fiddle, bodhrán and tin whistle open to anyone who wanders in.
thingsToDo.tip: Arrive early for a seat near the musicians in the more popular venues.

thingsToDo.title: Explore Dublin's literary history
thingsToDo.text: A rich trail connecting Joyce, Wilde, Beckett and Yeats, from statues and plaques to the Dublin Writers Museum.
thingsToDo.tip: A literary pub crawl combines the theme with a proper night out.

foodIntro: Dublin's food spans serious modern Irish dining and simple, hearty pub classics at every price point.

foods.name: A pint of Guinness

image.alt: A freshly poured pint of Guinness stout

foods.text: Tastes different at the source, poured fresh with the traditional two-part method across the city's pubs.
foods.whereToTry: Traditional pubs citywide, plus the Guinness Storehouse itself.

foods.name: Irish stew

image.alt: A bowl of hearty Irish stew

foods.text: Worth seeking out at a traditional pub, a simple, slow-cooked stew of lamb, potatoes and root vegetables.
foods.whereToTry: Traditional pubs and restaurants throughout the city centre.

foods.name: Full Irish breakfast

image.alt: A full Irish breakfast with rashers, sausages, egg and black pudding

foods.text: A substantial start to the day, found on nearly every café menu across the city.
foods.whereToTry: Cafés and hotel breakfasts throughout Dublin.

foods.name: Fish and chips

image.file: File:Fish and chips plate with peas.jpg
image.alt: A plate of fish and chips

foods.text: A reliable, hearty classic, sold at chippers across the city, especially popular after a night out.
foods.whereToTry: Chip shops citywide, particularly around Temple Bar and the north city centre.

foods.name: Irish soda bread

image.alt: A loaf of traditional Irish soda bread

foods.text: A daily staple, dense and slightly sweet, served alongside soup, stew or a simple breakfast.
foods.whereToTry: Cafés and bakeries throughout the city.

foods.name: Boxty

image.alt: Boxty, a traditional Irish potato pancake

foods.text: A traditional potato pancake, crisp outside and soft within, often served wrapped around a savoury filling.
foods.whereToTry: Traditional Irish restaurants around Temple Bar.

accommodation.intro: Dublin offers accommodation across every budget, concentrated within a compact, walkable city centre.

areas.name: City centre (south of the Liffey)
areas.bestFor: Being central and walkable to major sights
areas.text: The most convenient base, close to Trinity College, Grafton Street and Temple Bar.

areas.name: Docklands and north city centre
areas.text: A short walk or tram ride from the centre, with good access to Phoenix Park and the main train stations.

gettingThere.intro: Dublin is Ireland's main international gateway, well connected by air and sea.

options.text: Most international routes into Ireland land here, about 30 minutes from the city centre.
options.detail: Frequent express buses connect the airport to central Dublin around the clock.

options.text: A popular option for visitors bringing a car from Britain, docking at the nearby port of Dublin.
options.detail: Routes run from Holyhead and other UK ports.

options.text: Fast and direct from Cork, Galway, Kilkenny and other major towns.
options.detail: Trains arrive at Heuston or Connolly station, both close to the city centre.

gettingAround.intro: Dublin is compact enough to explore mostly on foot, with good public transport for the rest.

options.text: Covers Trinity College, Temple Bar, Dublin Castle and most of the city centre easily.
options.detail: Central Dublin's main sights sit within a comfortable walking radius of each other.

options.text: Reliable for reaching Phoenix Park, the docklands and other outer neighbourhoods.
options.detail: A single Leap Card covers trams, buses and the DART train.

options.text: The easiest way to reach Howth and the coastal suburbs.
options.detail: Runs frequently along the coast, both north and south of the city centre.

bestTime.headline: May to September for the best weather, though Dublin works well year-round
bestTime.summary: Dublin's museum-heavy, walkable character makes it a viable destination in any season, though summer brings the mildest outdoor conditions.

seasons.text: Mild weather and long daylight hours, with fewer crowds than midsummer.
The warmest and busiest season, with festivals and outdoor events, also the priciest time to visit.
Mild with thinner crowds than summer, a good balance for museum-heavy sightseeing.
Short days and frequent rain, though atmospheric, with cosy pubs and lower prices.

bestTime.avoid: Nothing strongly — Dublin's museum-rich, compact character makes it a workable destination in any season.

tipsIntro: Practical notes that make a Dublin stay noticeably smoother.
tips: Book Guinness Storehouse and Kilmainham Gaol tickets well ahead — both regularly sell out.
Get a Leap Card for easy, discounted travel on trams, buses and the DART.
Budget for high restaurant and pub prices, especially around Temple Bar.
Wear comfortable shoes — Dublin's compact centre still adds up to real walking distances.
Pack a proper waterproof layer regardless of season — Dublin's weather shifts fast.
Walk a few streets beyond Temple Bar for a quieter, cheaper, and often better pint.

faq.q: How many days do you need in Dublin?
faq.a: Two to three days covers the major museums and sights at a comfortable, unrushed pace.

faq.q: Is Dublin worth visiting before heading to the rest of Ireland?
faq.a: Yes — its museums and history add real context, and it's the natural gateway for trains and buses onward.
Yes, one of the more expensive parts of Ireland — self-catering and a guesthouse help manage costs.
Yes — most major sights sit within a comfortable walk of the city centre, with good public transport for the rest.
Its literary history, Trinity College and the Book of Kells, the Guinness Storehouse, and a legendary pub and live music culture.

faq.q: Do I need to book the Book of Kells in advance?
faq.a: Yes, strongly recommended — timed tickets for the Long Room and Book of Kells sell out, especially in summer.
